title: Šahrestānīhā ī Ērānšahr, the western quarter (§§21–33) with §12 — a Middle Persian catalogue of who founded which city, in which twenty-four of them are built partly by the King of Kings and partly by the Caesar, and Alexander is called a Roman
language_note:
Middle Persian (Pārsīg), `pal`, as persia-01-skz and persia-05-abnun carry it. WHAT IS REPRODUCED IS THE NORMALISED TRANSCRIPTION AND NOT THE PAHLAVI SCRIPT, AND THE REASON IS MECHANICAL RATHER THAN EDITORIAL. Parsīg Database renders the Book Pahlavi of each section in a mapped display font: the glyphs a reader sees are Pahlavi, and the characters underneath them are Arabic-script code points standing in for Pahlavi letters — the first section extracts as `فل‌ا‌ا‌ فقثم : صـت‌غج` and means nothing at those code points. Copying it would put mojibake in a retrieval-eligible chunk and label it a source text. THE TRANSCRIPTION IS THE SOURCE-LANGUAGE TEXT HERE, in the same sense that persia-05-abnun's normalised transcription is: it carries `*` on conjectural forms, `[ ]` on restorations and `< >` on editorial additions, and the editorial doubt is legible in it.

EIGHT CONJECTURAL FORMS ARE MARKED INSIDE THE EXCERPT — *warāzag twice, *az, *haft, and the sections' own asterisks — and none is silently resolved.
date: The text as it stands is post-762 CE and its material is late Sasanian. Section 60, outside this excerpt, credits the founding of Baghdad to `abūgāfar` — Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, `čiyōn-išān abūdawānīg xwānd`, whom they called Abū Dawānīq — which cannot be earlier than 762 CE, so the redaction is early Abbasid. Inside the excerpt, §33 names Kūfa, Mecca and Medina beside Syria and Yemen, and §32 credits nine cities of upper Mesopotamia to a nephew of the Caesar. THE DATE THIS RECORD ASSERTS IS THE DATE OF THE REDACTION AND NOT OF ANY SECTION IN IT: a catalogue that names Yima and al-Manṣūr in one list is not datable section by section from anything on the page, and this record does not date it section by section.

THE CAPTURE IS NOT BLIND AND THAT IS DECLARED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED. This session located the source, read the transcription and read the English in the same pass, so the paste is not checked against an independent second reading — it is one reading, transcribed once. `F6_BROWSER_PASS2.md` deliberately stopped at the interface and did NOT open the text, precisely so that a later blind paste would be possible; the curation then happened in the same session anyway, and it is the pass, not the record, that kept its half of the rule. Same declaration as browser pass 1 and southasia-05. FINDING 55's principle applies in full: this record's own consistency is worth nothing as evidence about it.

EDITORIAL ACTS, DECLARED. The two bracketed headings and the note that §12 is out of sequence are supplied by this record. The section numbers, the hyphen after them, the `*`, `[ ]` and `< >` markers and the per-section `(Jamasp-Asana, 1913, p.NN)` citations are the database's own and are kept exactly. The Persian translation that sits between the transcription and the English on the page is NOT reproduced: it is a third register in a fourth language and the corpus has no role for it. Nothing else is altered.

THE EXCERPT IS BOUNDED AND THE BOUNDARY IS AN ARGUMENT. §§21–33 are CONTIGUOUS — the whole of the `kust ī xwarwarān`, the western quarter, from Ctesiphon to the twenty-four cities of Syria, Yemen and Africa. Nothing inside that run is dropped, including §§28–30 on the mountain-rulers of Padišxwārgar, which say nothing about Rome. Taking the quarter whole rather than the four Roman sentences out of it is the difference between quoting a text and assembling one. §12 is taken separately, out of sequence, is labelled as such, and is one sentence.

WHAT DID NOT GO WRONG, CHECKED BEFORE THE RECORD WAS WRITTEN. Every diacritic is precomposed NFC — ā ē ī ō ū š č ǰ ṣ — and the `ī` of the ubiquitous ezāfe is U+012B throughout. The angle brackets of `<ud>` in §32 and `<ī>` in §24 survive as ASCII `<` `>`. The `-ē` of `wīst-ē` and `šahrestān-ē` uses U+002D, not an en dash.
reference_translation:
[THE WESTERN QUARTER — sections 21 to 33]

21- In the quarter of the West, Varāza son of Gēv built by the order of Tusa the city of Ctesiphon. (Asha, n.d.)

22- Varāza son of Gēv built the city of Nisibis. (Asha, n.d.)

23- Narsē the Arsacian built the city of Edessa. (Asha, n.d.)

24- Babylon built the city of Babylon during the reign of Yima. He fettered there the planet Tīr (Mercury). And he showed the account of the seven and the twelve, that is, [the astrology of] the constellations and planets, and the eighth tower (sky of the fixed stars), by sorcery to Miθra of Babylon. (Asha, n.d.)

25- Šābuhr son of Ardašēr built the city of Hērt (Ḥīra), and he appointed Mihrzād the margrave of Hērt on the “desert” of the Arabs. (Asha, n.d.)

26- Yazdegird son of Šābuhr whom they call Yazdegird the rough built the city of Hamadān (Ecbatana). (Asha, n.d.)

27- Vahrām son of Yazdegird whom they have called Vahrām gōr (‘the onager’) built a city in [the land of] Māy-kust-ī-nihāvand [called ] Var ī Vahrāmāvand. (Asha, n.d.)

28- The twenty-one cities which have been built in Pedišxvārgar, either Armāyēl [himself] built [some] or else some were built, at the order of Armāyēl, by the mountain-rulers who from Aži Dahāka had obtained the dominion of the mountains [of Pedišxvārgar]. (Asha, n.d.)

29- There are seven mountain-rulers: Dumbāvand Visēmagān; Nahagān; Visped; Naxvdārān; Vimanddāragān; bln/w/cʾn; mlyn/w/cʾn. (Asha, n.d.)

30- These were those who from Aži Dahāka had obtained mountains for kingship. (Asha, n.d.)

31- Pērōz son of Šābuhr built the city of Mosul. (Asha, n.d.)

32- The nine cities which have been built in the land of Mesopotamia Superior, Amidos, the nephew of Caesar, built them. (Asha, n.d.)

33- The twenty-four cities which exist in the lands of Syria, Yemen, and Africa, Kūfa and Mecca and Medina, some [were built] by the king of kings and some by the Caesar. (Asha, n.d.)

[SECTION 12]

12- The accursed Alexander the Greek built the city of Marv and the city of Herat (Harē/ Areia). (Asha, n.d.)

WHERE THE TRANSLATION AND THE SOURCE TEXT DO NOT SAY THE SAME THING, AND IT IS NOT ARGUED HERE. THREE PLACES, ALL INSIDE THE EXCERPT ABOVE, ALL VISIBLE TO A READER WHO HAS BOTH CHUNKS IN FRONT OF THEM:

(a) SECTION 12. The Middle Persian is `gizistag skandar ī hrōmāyīg` and the published English is “the accursed Alexander the Greek”. The word in the text is `hrōmāyīg` — the adjective this corpus's other Persian records carry as ROMAN, as `Hrōmāy` in persia-05-abnun's `Hrōmāy abar Pārs ud Pahlaw āyēnd`. The translator's reading is defensible: in Middle Persian usage Hrōm covers the Greek-speaking eastern empire and a Sasanian writer calling Alexander `hrōmāyīg` is not making a claim about the city of Rome. IT IS STILL A CHOICE, and this record makes no other. What it does is put both words in front of the reader and say that the second is the first translated.

(b) SECTION 28. The transcription reads `wīst-ē šahestān` and the English reads “The twenty-one cities”. The same `wīst-ē` opens section 33, where it is followed by `čahār` and rendered “twenty-four”. Whether the `-ē` of section 28 is a counted unit or the indefinite enclitic is exactly the kind of question this record cannot settle and does not try to.

(c) SECTION 29. The transcription names seven mountain-rulers and so does the English, but the English leaves the last two UNREAD — `bln/w/cʾn` and `mlyn/w/cʾn` — printed in the consonantal skeleton rather than in a reading, where the transcription has `barōzān` and `marinzān`. The translator declines twice where the transcriber does not. That divergence is the source's own and is reproduced, not repaired.

Sogdiana has seven settlements,` — a clause that belongs to §6, which then begins `and its having seven settlements means...`; and §55's English ends with a whole sentence duplicated from §50, `...and brought the land of Simrān back into the possession of Ērānšahr, and conveyed the Arabian plain as a personal inherited possession to Bādesrū, the Arab king, so that his descendants should [also] possess it.` NOTHING INSIDE §§12 AND 21–33 SHOWS THE DEFECT, and every section in the excerpt was read against its own transcription for it. Reported, not repaired, and not counted: no attempt was made to audit the other forty-seven sections.

notes:
F6, and Persia's re-pointed slot. RULING 76 turned F6's Persia `published_translation_only` slot into a `verbatim_with_provenance` slot for one reason: FINDING 71 had shown Persia ending Block F at 3 source-language records against a floor of 4 BY CONSTRUCTION, with both its remaining slots on tiers that do not count toward the floor and no Persia slot anywhere in F7. THIS RECORD IS WHAT MOVES THAT FLOOR FROM UNREACHABLE TO MET, and it is the only record in the whole remaining allocation that could have.

WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT ROME, AND WHY IT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF EVIDENCE FROM THE TWO PERSIAN RECORDS ALREADY HERE. persia-01-skz is a king's account of beating the Romans and persia-05-abnun is a courtier's vow that the king will. BOTH ARE ABOUT A WAR. This is an administrative list, and Rome appears in it as an ordinary fact of the world:

  §32  the nine cities of upper Mesopotamia were built by `āmitūs <ud> kēsar brādar-zād` — Amidos, the NEPHEW OF CAESAR.
  §33  of twenty-four cities in Syria, Yemen, Africa, Kūfa, Mecca and Medina, `ast šāhān šāh ast kēsar` — SOME BY THE KING OF KINGS, SOME BY THE CAESAR.
  §22  Nisibis and §23 Edessa, the two cities the Roman and Persian empires spent three centuries exchanging, are here simply founded by a son of Gēv and by Narsē the Arsacian.
  §12  Alexander is `gizistag skandar ī hrōmāyīg` — the accursed Alexander THE ROMAN.

§33 IS THE SENTENCE. A Middle Persian geography divides the city-founding of the whole known world between two builders and names them in the same breath, with no verb of conflict between them: the King of Kings and the Caesar, as the two agents by whom cities come to exist. That is the Roman empire seen from Ērānšahr as a PEER INSTITUTION rather than as an adversary, and this corpus did not previously hold a Persian text that said so.

NOT DECLARED GLOSS-CAPABLE, AND THE MATERIAL FOR ONE IS SITTING IN IT. §12's `hrōmāyīg` rendered `the Greek`, §28's `wīst-ē` rendered `twenty-one`, and §29's two names the translator leaves unread are three genuine divergences between two chunks a reader meets together, and all three are inside `reference_translation` where the loader chunks them. F6's allocation carries exactly ONE gloss_capable declaration and RULING 77 spends it on CIH 541. A second declaration here would be over-delivery on a quota, which check_delivery fails on the day it happens. RECORDED SO THAT F7 CAN TAKE IT: if F7 needs a gloss-capable record and its own candidates fail, the divergence is already in the corpus and already in a retrieval-eligible chunk.

THE HONEST WEAKNESS, AND IT IS THE TRANSLATION SEARCH. Daryaee 2002 is by its own title an English translation of exactly this text with commentary, it is named in the bibliography printed on the source's own record page, and IT WAS NOT OPENED. This record cites the English that was on the page beside the text. `translation_source` states that boundary in the words this tier requires and does not dress it up as a finding about what exists.

THE SECOND WEAKNESS IS THE CAPTURE PATH. The locating pass and the capture happened in one session, so nothing independent checked the paste. Declared in `original_text_note` rather than mitigated.

WHAT WAS REJECTED FOR THIS SLOT, AND WHY, so that F7 does not re-hunt it. `zand ī wahman yasn` — on the same site, complete, with English, and it names Hrōm in its apocalyptic sequence — was passed over because its edited text is Anklesaria 1957 and the rights position of a 1957 edition is a question this record would have had to answer with the site's two contradictory sentences and nothing else; `šahrīhā ī ērān` rests on Jamasp-Asana 1897–1913 instead. `abdīh ud sahīgīh ī sīstān` rests on the same public-domain edition and has English, and is a live F7 candidate for Persia's re-pointed catalogue slot. The Manichaean Middle Persian corpus behind Boyce 1975 is 59 keyed texts with manuscript facsimiles from the Turfan archive and IS NOT PERSIA under this corpus's findspot rule — Turfan finds are East Asia, which is the mis-regioning F6 inherited over `M2 I` and `M 5794 I` and which this record does not settle either.

subject_places.name: Tīsifōn (tīsifōn, Ctesiphon)
subject_places.note: §21 names it as the first city of the western quarter and the excerpt is organised as a walk outward from it. Pleiades 893976, titled `Ctesiphon`, locationPrecision `precise`, hull spanning -540..2000 and attesting `roman-early-empire-parthian-middle-east` and `late-antique-sasanian-middle-east` — both inside this project's window. `stated` because the text names it.

subject_places.name: Nasībīn (nasībīn, Nisibis)
subject_places.note: §22. Pleiades 874623 `Nisibis/Antiochia`, locationPrecision `precise`, -330..1599, attesting `roman` and `late-antique`. TWO OTHER PLEIADES RECORDS CARRY THE NAME AND ARE REFUSED: 60591 and 897813 are both `unlocated` Nisibis entries derived from literary attestation, and this text is about the city that exists on the ground at modern Nusaybin. A name match is not an identification; the coordinate and description were read before the id was taken.

subject_places.name: Ōrhāy (ōrhāy, Edessa)
subject_places.note: §23. Pleiades 658457 `Edessa/Antiochia ad Callirhoem`, locationPrecision `precise`, attesting `roman-early-empire-parthian-middle-east` and `late-antique-sasanian-middle-east`. PLEIADES 491585 `Edessa (Macedonia)` IS REFUSED and is named here because it is the trap: it is a `precise` entry, it attests `roman`, and it is the wrong Edessa. The Middle Persian `ōrhāy` is Urhāy/Urfa, in upper Mesopotamia, which is 658457.

subject_places.name: kēsar — the Caesar
subject_places.note: §32 and §33. NO ID IS TAKEN, AND SPECIFICALLY PLEIADES 423025 `Roma` IS NOT IMPORTED HERE. The text names an OFFICE and not a city: `kēsar`, the Caesar, twice, as the builder of cities in Mesopotamia, Syria, Yemen and Africa. persia-05-abnun made the same refusal for `Hrōmāy`, the Romans as a people, and gave the reason this record repeats: arabia-06-syllaeus carries 423025 because its Safaitic text says `rm`, the place. Converting a title into a city would be this project supplying the geography its source declines to. `regional` with no id, and the map is sparser for it.

subject_places.name: zamīg gazīrag — the land of upper Mesopotamia (the Jazīra)
subject_places.note: §32, the nine cities built by the Caesar's nephew. `regional` with no id: `gazīrag` is the Jazīra, a region rather than a settlement, and the pinned 2026-08-10 dump was not searched for a region entry matching it. NOT SEARCHED AND NOT FOUND ARE TWO DIFFERENT THINGS and this note says which.

subject_places.name: šām, yaman, frīgā, kufah, makka, madīnag — Syria, Yemen, Africa, Kūfa, Mecca, Medina
subject_places.note: §33, the twenty-four cities `ast šāhān šāh ast kēsar`. SIX NAMES, NO IDS, AND THE REFUSAL IS DELIBERATE RATHER THAN LAZY. The sentence does not say which of the six the Caesar built and which the King of Kings built; placing all six would put the Roman emperor on a map of Mecca and Medina on this record's authority, which is precisely the thing the text declines to specify. The corpus loses six pins and keeps the sentence's own vagueness, which is the information.

subject_places.name: Marw and Harē (marw, harē — Merv and Herat)
subject_places.note: §12, the two cities founded by `skandar ī hrōmāyīg`. `regional` WITH NO ID, AND THE GROUND WAS CORRECTED RATHER THAN THE ID SUPPLIED. It was first written `stated`, on the reasoning that the text names both cities; the schema refused it, because `stated` on a SPECIFIC place requires an id and the honest ground without one is `regional`. That refusal is right and the reason to keep the ground rather than go and find the ids is the excerpt's own frame: §12 is taken out of the eastern quarter for ONE ADJECTIVE in it, `hrōmāyīg`, and pinning Merv and Herat would be placing a sentence this record quotes for a word. Recorded by name. If F7 takes the eastern quarter, the ids are worth finding then.
